danish.title: Tolvte bog (1812) — Kapitel 8
paragraphs: Sonjas brev, skrevet fra Tróitsa, som var kommet som svar på Nikolajs bøn, var foranlediget af følgende: tanken om at få Nikolaj gift med en arving optog den gamle grevindes sind mere og mere. Hun vidste, at Sonja var den vigtigste hindring herfor, og Sonjas liv i grevindens hus var blevet hårdere og hårdere, især efter at de havde modtaget et brev fra Nikolaj, der fortalte om hans møde med prinsesse Marja i Bogutjárovo. Grevinden lod ingen lejlighed gå forbi til at komme med ydmygende eller grusomme hentydninger til Sonja.

Men et par dage før de forlod Moskva kaldte grevinden, bevæget og ophidset af alt det, der foregik, Sonja til sig og bønfaldt hende i stedet for at bebrejde og stille krav tårevædet om at ofre sig og gengælde alt, hvad familien havde gjort for hende, ved at bryde sin forlovelse med Nikolaj.
»Jeg får ikke ro, før du lover mig det.«

Sonja brast i hysterisk gråd og svarede gennem sin hulken, at hun ville gøre alt og var parat til alt, men gav intet egentligt løfte og kunne ikke bringe sig selv til at gøre, hvad der forlangtes af hende. Hun måtte ofre sig for den familie, der havde opdraget hende. At ofre sig for andre var Sonjas vane. Hendes stilling i huset var sådan, at hun kun ved selvopofrelse kunne vise sit værd, og hun var vant til det og elskede at gøre det. Men i alle sine tidligere selvopofrelses-handlinger havde hun med glæde været bevidst om, at de løftede hende i hendes egne og andres øjne og derved gjorde hende mere værdig til Nikolaj, som hun elskede over alt i verden. Men nu forlangte de, at hun skulle ofre netop det, der udgjorde hele belønningen for hendes selvopofrelse og hele meningen med hendes liv. Og for første gang følte hun bitterhed mod dem, der kun havde været hendes velgørere for at pine hende desto smerteligere; hun følte jalousi over for Natasja, der aldrig havde oplevet noget lignende, aldrig havde haft behov for at ofre sig, men fik andre til at ofre sig for sig og alligevel var elsket af alle. Og for første gang følte Sonja, at der ud af hendes rene, stille kærlighed til Nikolaj voksede en lidenskabelig følelse, der var stærkere end principper, dyd eller religion. Under indflydelse af denne følelse besluttede Sonja, hvis liv i afhængighed havde lært hende ufrivilligt at være hemmelighedsfuld, efter at have svaret grevinden i vage vendinger at undgå at tale med hende og afvente mødet med Nikolaj, ikke for at sætte ham fri, men tværtimod for ved dette møde at binde ham til sig for evigt.

Urolighederne og rædslen i Rostov-familiens sidste dage i Moskva kvalte de dystre tanker, der trykkede Sonja. Hun var glad for at finde tilflugt fra dem i praktisk virksomhed. Men da hun hørte om fyrst Andrejs tilstedeværelse i deres hus, blev hun trods sin oprigtige medlidenhed med ham og med Natasja grebet af en glad og overtroisk følelse af, at Gud ikke havde til hensigt at skille hende fra Nikolaj. Hun vidste, at Natasja ikke elskede andre end fyrst Andrej og aldrig havde holdt op med at elske ham. Hun vidste, at når de atter blev kastet sammen under så forfærdelige omstændigheder, ville de igen forelske sig i hinanden, og at Nikolaj så ikke ville kunne gifte sig med prinsesse Marja, da de ville komme inden for de forbudte slægtskabsgrader. Trods al rædslen over det, der var sket i de seneste dage og under rejsens første dage, opmuntrede denne følelse af, at Forsynet greb ind i hendes personlige anliggender, Sonja.
Ved Tróitsa-klosteret holdt Rostov-familien for første gang hvil en hel dag.

Tre store værelser blev tildelt dem i klostrets herberge, og et af dem var optaget af fyrst Andrej. Den sårede havde det meget bedre den dag, og Natasja sad hos ham. I det tilstødende værelse sad greven og grevinden og samtalte respektfuldt med prioren, der aflagde besøg hos dem som gamle bekendte og velgørere af klostret. Sonja var der også, plaget af nysgerrighed efter hvad fyrst Andrej og Natasja talte om. Hun hørte lyden af deres stemmer gennem døren. Den dør åbnede sig, og Natasja kom ud med ophidset mine. Uden at lægge mærke til munken, der var rejst sig for at hilse på hende, og som trak det brede ærme på sin højre arm tilbage, gik hun hen til Sonja og tog hendes hånd.
»Natasja, hvad laver du? Kom herhen!« sagde grevinden.
Natasja gik hen til munken for at modtage hans velsignelse, og han rådede hende til at bede Gud og hans helgen om hjælp.
Så snart prioren havde trukket sig tilbage, tog Natasja sin veninde i hånden og gik med hende ind i det tomme værelse.

»Sonja, mon han lever?« spurgte hun. »Sonja, hvor er jeg lykkelig, og hvor er jeg ulykkelig!... Sonja, duen min, alt er som det plejede at være. Bare han lever! Det kan han ikke... fordi... fordi... af...« og Natasja brast i gråd.
»Ja! Det vidste jeg! Gudskelov!« mumlede Sonja. »Han lever.«

Sonja var ikke mindre bevæget end sin veninde af dennes frygt og sorg og af sine egne personlige følelser, som hun ikke delte med nogen. Hulkende kyssede og trøstede hun Natasja. »Bare han lever!« tænkte hun. Da de havde grædt, talt og tørret deres tårer, gik de to veninder sammen hen til fyrst Andrejs dør. Natasja åbnede den forsigtigt og kiggede ind i værelset, mens Sonja stod ved siden af hende ved den halvåbne dør.
Fyrst Andrej lå højt løftet på tre puder. Hans blege ansigt var roligt, hans øjne lukkede, og de kunne se hans regelmæssige åndedrag.
»Åh, Natasja!« udbrød Sonja pludselig næsten skrigende, greb sin venindes arm og trådte tilbage fra døren.
»Hvad? Hvad er der?« spurgte Natasja.
»Det er det, det...« sagde Sonja med hvidt ansigt og skælvende læber.
Natasja lukkede stille døren og gik med Sonja hen til vinduet, uden endnu at forstå, hvad den anden fortalte hende.
»Husker du,« sagde Sonja med højtideligt og skræmt udtryk. »Husker du, da jeg kiggede i spejlet for dig... i Otrádnoje ved jul? Husker du, hvad jeg så?«
»Ja, ja!« udbrød Natasja og spilede øjnene op, mens hun vagt mindedes, at Sonja havde fortalt hende noget om fyrst Andrej, som hun havde set ligge ned.

»Husker du?« fortsatte Sonja. »Jeg så det dengang og fortalte alle, dig og Dunjásja. Jeg så ham ligge på en seng,« sagde hun og gestikulerede med hånden og løftede en finger ved hver detalje, »og at han havde lukkede øjne og var dækket af netop et lyserødt tæppe, og at hans hænder var foldede,« sluttede hun og overbeviste sig selv om, at de detaljer, hun netop havde set, var nøjagtigt, hvad hun havde set i spejlet.

I virkeligheden havde hun dengang slet intet set, men havde nævnt det første, der faldt hende ind, men det, hun havde opfundet dengang, forekom hende nu lige så virkeligt som enhver anden erindring. Hun huskede ikke blot, hvad hun dengang havde sagt — at han vendte sig for at se på hende og smilede, og at han var dækket med noget rødt — men var fast overbevist om, at hun dengang havde set og sagt, at han var dækket med et lyserødt tæppe, og at hans øjne var lukkede.
»Ja, ja, det var virkelig lyserødt!« udbrød Natasja, som nu troede, at også hun huskede, at ordet lyserødt var blevet brugt, og i dette så den mest ekstraordinære og mystiske del af forudsigelsen.
»Men hvad betyder det?« tilføjede hun eftertænksomt.
»Åh, jeg ved det ikke, det hele er så mærkeligt,« svarede Sonja og greb sig til hovedet.
Et par minutter senere ringede fyrst Andrej, og Natasja gik ind til ham, men Sonja, usædvanligt oprevet og rørt, blev ved vinduet og grublede over det mærkelige, der var sket.
De fik den dag lejlighed til at sende breve til hæren, og grevinden var i færd med at skrive til sin søn.

»Sonja!« sagde grevinden og løftede øjnene fra brevet, da hendes niece passerede, »Sonja, vil du ikke skrive til Nikolaj?« Hun talte med en blød, skælvende stemme, og i de trætte øjne, der så over brillerne, læste Sonja alt det, grevinden mente med disse ord. De øjne udtrykte bøn, skam over at måtte bede, frygt for et afslag og parathed til ubønhørligt had i tilfælde af et sådant afslag.
Sonja gik hen til grevinden og kyssede knælende hendes hånd.
»Ja, Mamma, jeg vil skrive,« sagde hun.

Sonja var blødgjort, bevæget og rørt af alt, hvad der var sket den dag, især af den mystiske opfyldelse af sin vision, hun netop havde været vidne til. Nu da hun vidste, at fornyelsen af Natasjas forhold til fyrst Andrej ville forhindre Nikolaj i at gifte sig med prinsesse Marja, var hun med glæde bevidst om et tilbagevenden af den selvopofrelse, hun var vant til at leve i og elskede at leve i. Så med en glad bevidsthed om at udføre en ædelmodig handling — afbrudt flere gange af de tårer, der slørede hendes fløjlssorte øjne — skrev hun det rørende brev, hvis ankomst havde overrasket Nikolaj så stærkt.

english.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: Sonya's letter from Troitsa, which had come as an answer to Nicholas' prayer, had a cause. The old countess thought more and more about marrying Nicholas to an heiress. She knew Sonya was the main obstacle, and Sonya's life in the countess' house had grown harder and harder, especially after a letter from Nicholas told of his meeting with Princess Mary at Bogucharovo. The countess never let a chance slip to make humiliating or cruel remarks about Sonya.

But a few days before they left Moscow, moved and stirred up by everything going on around her, she called Sonya to her. Instead of reproaching her and making demands, she tearfully begged her to sacrifice herself and repay all the family had done for her by breaking off her engagement to Nicholas.
"I shan't be at peace until you promise me this."

Sonya burst into hysterical tears. Between sobs she answered that she would do anything and was ready for anything, but she made no actual promise and couldn't bring herself to decide to do what was asked. She had to sacrifice herself for the family that had raised and brought her up. Sacrificing herself for others was Sonya's habit. Her position in the house was such that only through sacrifice could she show her worth, and she was used to this and loved doing it. But in all her earlier acts of self-sacrifice she had been happily aware that they raised her in her own eyes and in others', and so made her more worthy of Nicholas, whom she loved more than anything in the world. Now they wanted her to sacrifice the very thing that was the whole reward of her self-sacrifice and the whole meaning of her life. For the first time she felt bitter toward those who had been her benefactors only to torture her the more painfully. She felt jealous of Natasha, who had never experienced anything like this, had never needed to sacrifice herself, but made others sacrifice themselves for her, and was loved by everybody all the same. And for the first time Sonya felt that her pure, quiet love for Nicholas was beginning to grow into a passionate feeling stronger than principle, virtue or religion. Under the influence of this feeling, Sonya, whose life of dependence had taught her without her meaning it to be secretive, answered the countess in vague general terms and avoided talking with her. She resolved to wait until she saw Nicholas, and then, not to set him free but on the contrary to bind him to her forever.

The bustle and terror of the Rostovs' last days in Moscow smothered the gloomy thoughts that weighed on Sonya. She was glad to escape from them into practical activity. But when she heard that Prince Andrew was in their house, then, despite her sincere pity for him and for Natasha, a joyful and superstitious feeling seized her: God did not intend her to be separated from Nicholas. She knew that Natasha loved no one but Prince Andrew and had never stopped loving him. She knew that, thrown together again in such terrible circumstances, they would fall in love with each other again, and that Nicholas would then be unable to marry Princess Mary, since they would be within the prohibited degrees of affinity. Despite all the terror of what had happened in those last days and in the first days of their journey, this feeling that Providence was stepping into her personal affairs cheered Sonya.
At the Troitsa monastery the Rostovs stopped for a whole day, their first break in the journey.

They were given three large rooms in the monastery hostelry, and Prince Andrew occupied one of them. The wounded man was much better that day, and Natasha was sitting with him. In the next room the count and countess sat talking respectfully with the prior, who was calling on them as old acquaintances and benefactors of the monastery. Sonya was there too, tormented by curiosity about what Prince Andrew and Natasha were saying. She could hear their voices through the door. The door opened and Natasha came out, looking excited. She didn't notice the monk, who had risen to greet her and was drawing back the wide sleeve of his right arm. She went straight up to Sonya and took her hand.
"Natasha, what are you doing? Come here!" said the countess.
Natasha went to the monk for his blessing, and he advised her to pray for help to God and His saint.
As soon as the prior withdrew, Natasha took her friend by the hand and led her into the empty room.

"Sonya, will he live?" she asked. "Sonya, how happy I am, and how unhappy!... Sonya, dovey, everything is as it used to be. If only he lives! He can't... because... because... of..." and Natasha burst into tears.
"Yes! I knew it! Thank God!" murmured Sonya. "He will live."

Sonya was as shaken as her friend, both by Natasha's fear and grief and by her own feelings, which she shared with no one. She kissed Natasha, sobbing, and comforted her. "If only he lives!" she thought. When they had wept, talked and wiped away their tears, the two friends went together to Prince Andrew's door. Natasha opened it carefully and peeped into the room, with Sonya beside her at the half-open door.
Prince Andrew was lying propped up on three pillows. His pale face was calm and his eyes were closed, and they could see that he was breathing evenly.
"Oh, Natasha!" Sonya suddenly almost screamed, catching her companion's arm and stepping back from the door.
"What? What is it?" asked Natasha.
"It's that, that..." said Sonya, white-faced, her lips trembling.
Natasha quietly closed the door and went with Sonya to the window, not yet understanding what Sonya was trying to tell her.
"You remember," said Sonya, with a solemn, frightened look. "You remember when I looked in the mirror for you... at Otradnoe at Christmas? Do you remember what I saw?"
"Yes, yes!" cried Natasha, opening her eyes wide. She vaguely recalled that Sonya had told her something about Prince Andrew, whom she had seen lying down.

"You remember?" Sonya went on. "I saw it then and told everybody, you and Dunyasha. I saw him lying on a bed," she said, making a gesture with her hand and lifting a finger at each detail, "and he had his eyes closed and was covered with just a pink quilt, and his hands were folded," she finished, convincing herself that the details she had just seen were exactly what she had seen in the mirror.

In fact she had seen nothing then and had simply said the first thing that came into her head. But what she had invented then seemed as real to her now as any other memory. She not only remembered what she had said then (that he turned to look at her and smiled, and was covered with something red), but was firmly convinced that she had seen and said then that he was covered with a pink quilt and that his eyes were closed.
"Yes, yes, it really was pink!" cried Natasha, who now thought she too remembered the word pink being used, and saw in this the most extraordinary and mysterious part of the prediction.
"But what does it mean?" she added thoughtfully.
"Oh, I don't know, it's all so strange," replied Sonya, clutching her head.
A few minutes later Prince Andrew rang, and Natasha went to him. Sonya, feeling unusually excited and moved, stayed at the window, thinking about how strange it all was.
That day they had a chance to send letters to the army, and the countess was writing to her son.

"Sonya!" said the countess, raising her eyes from her letter as her niece passed. "Sonya, won't you write to Nicholas?" She spoke in a soft, trembling voice, and in the weary eyes that looked over her spectacles Sonya read everything the countess meant by these words. Those eyes showed entreaty, shame at having to ask, fear of a refusal, and readiness for relentless hatred if she were refused.
Sonya went up to the countess and, kneeling, kissed her hand.
"Yes, Mamma, I will write," she said.

Sonya was softened, excited and moved by everything that had happened that day, above all by the mysterious fulfillment of her vision, which she had just witnessed. She now knew that the renewal of Natasha's relations with Prince Andrew would stop Nicholas from marrying Princess Mary. She was joyfully aware that the self-sacrificing spirit she was used to living in, and loved living in, had come back to her. So, with the joyful feeling of doing a magnanimous deed, and stopping several times as tears dimmed her velvety black eyes, she wrote the touching letter whose arrival had so amazed Nicholas.
